activities.anchor: roughly 43% of people use two or more languages in daily life
activities.caption: call the share — the world's normal mind
activities.name: mcShareEstimate

config.prompt: Roughly what share of humanity manages more than one language every day?
config.why: About 43 per cent — so monolingualism, not multilingualism, is the global minority condition, and billions of bilinguals also read in two different scripts. The field studies the world's normal mind, not an exception.
config.context: Which is why every 'bilingual advantage' finding is a claim about most of humanity, not a special case.

activities.anchor: one symbol reliably equals one timing unit
activities.caption: file each script by the unit it writes
activities.name: mcScriptBuckets

config.prompt: Each script strikes its own deal between sound and symbol — file each by the unit of writing:

items.label: the Latin deal, before English corrupts it with history-over-pronunciation spellings
Cyrillic, sibling of the Latin arrangement
Devanagari: a base sign with its default vowel, diacritics overwriting it
hiragana, one of ~46 basic signs per beat

config.why: Alphabets write phonemes, abugidas and moraic syllabaries write syllable-sized units, Han writes morphemes — and how deep the deal runs decides how many school years reading takes to learn.

activities.anchor: Seymour, Aro and Erskine's 2003 cross-European study
activities.caption: place the years deep orthographies demand
activities.name: mcDepthPlace

config.prompt: Transparent orthographies reach near-ceiling reading within the first school year. When do deep-orthography learners match that accuracy?
config.why: Two to four years — and diagnosed dyslexia runs higher and resolves more slowly in deep-orthography countries. Brain imaging echoes it: Chinese reading recruits left middle frontal regions, alphabetic reading leans on the occipito-temporal visual word form area.
config.context: Same cognitive goal, different neural division of labour — the script is part of the reading skill.

activities.anchor: Pictographs (山 mountain, 木 tree) are a tiny minority
activities.caption: find the line the picture-myth would love
activities.name: mcHanSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is the picture-myth speaking — click it:
lines: Han characters map to morphemes — units of meaning-sound.
Roughly 80% or more of characters are phono-semantic compounds.
A meaning radical (water 氵) pairs with a sound component (工 → 江).
Chinese characters are mostly drawings of the things they name.
A literate reader can often pronounce a character never seen before.
config.correction: Almost none are drawings — sound components let readers pronounce unseen characters.
config.why: Because the compounds encode pronunciation as well as meaning, learning Han is massive and systematic, not merely photographic memory.

activities.caption: pair each experiment with what it exposed
activities.name: mcEvidenceMatch

config.prompt: Parallel activation, experiment by experiment — pair the observation with what it shows:

pairs.right: the co-activated other language keeps sound-alike candidates alive

pairs.left: FIN read with its Spanish meaning mid-English
switches land where both grammars agree
pairs.right: code-switching as constrained control — Poplack's equivalence constraint, not leakage

pairs.left: no clean on/off state between languages
pairs.right: a continuously weighted competition that a control network manages

config.why: The brain never switches languages off — which is why a fluent mid-sentence switch is skill, not confusion.

config.root: A worried parent: 'We are raising our daughter in two languages — everyone says she will end up delayed.' You have the research.

start.text: First claim on the table: two languages slow a child down. What do the controlled studies actually report?

choices.label: Development runs late in bilingual homes
choices.feedback: That is the folklore — and it fails under control.

choices.label: Development follows the usual timetable
choices.feedback: Correct — and what 'smaller vocabulary' really is, is the interesting part.

choices.label: It depends which two languages
choices.feedback: No pair-specific escape hatch exists in the data.

late.text: The delay story does not survive controlled comparison — there is nothing to trade away, so start again from the evidence.

vocab.text: At a given age, each single language looks smaller than a monolingual's. What does the combined total show?

choices.label: Combined vocabulary matches monolingual totals
choices.feedback: Two words for one concept were being counted once each — a sampling artefact, not a deficit.

choices.label: A smaller single language proves harm
choices.feedback: Follow the counting, not the intuition.

sampling.text: A quiet vocabulary-in-each-language score is a sampling artefact: the same concept often carries a word in both languages, so each list looks short.

choices.label: Ask about the mixing, then
choices.feedback: One more piece of the picture.

mixing.text: 'Juice-ju' style blends track monolingual children's transitional errors and fade on the same timetable — the mixed phase is a stage, not a symptom.

config.why: No delay: the usual developmental timetable, combined word-learning at par, blends that fade like every toddler's transitional errors.

activities.anchor: The story worth teaching is a case study
activities.caption: line up forty years of the debate
activities.name: mcDebateOrder

config.prompt: The advantage debate, from first claim to honest position — order the arc, earliest first:
items: Bialystok's flanker and Simon studies report bilinguals outperforming on executive control (1980s–2000s)
A widely cited 2007 paper claims bilingualism delays dementia symptoms by about four years
The replication era: registry-scale samples with tens of thousands of participants
Lehtonen's 2018 meta-analysis of 271 studies — the advantage mostly vanishes once confounds are controlled
The honest position: practical and social benefits stay robust — two cultures, and measurably faster third-language acquisition
config.why: The classic confounds — socioeconomic status, immigration history, publication bias — skew bilingual samples in many countries; Cenoz's L3 result is the cognitive benefit that survived, because the metalinguistic infrastructure is already built.

activities.anchor: speakers of any language can learn any concept
activities.caption: drag the divider — prison versus lens
activities.name: mcWhorfCompare

config.prompt: One hypothesis, two strengths — drag the divider:

before.label: Determinism — language imprisons thought
before.text: Disproved: every concept stays reachable from any tongue, and the limits on colour perception are set by the visual system, not the vocabulary.

after.label: Relativity — a lens with priorities
after.text: Well-replicated: Russian speakers discriminate the goluboy–siniy boundary about 10% faster, the edge vanishes under verbal interference (it runs through language, not perception), and Guugu Yimithirr speakers keep cardinal-direction orientation even indoors.

config.why: Kay and Kempton found English speakers over-discriminate near the green/blue name boundary — influence on salience and speed, never imprisonment.
